ReflectiChain: Grounding Long-Horizon
LLM Planning against Semantic-Execution Drift
Jia Luo
Abstract—In long-horizon dynamic environments, LLM agents
suffer from “Semantic-Execution Drift,” systematically reinter-
preting and violating initial language constraints under physical
pressure in pursuit of local success. Existing text-based reasoning
paradigms lack physical grounding and temporal alignment,
leading to constraint collapse. To address this problem, we pro-
pose ReflectiChain, a framework that reformulates constrained
planning as a trajectory-level reasoning problem by integrating
an implicit latent world model with a retrospective reflection
mechanism. By anticipating physical dynamics through latent
rollouts and re-anchoring drifting states to the original semantic
boundaries, ReflectiChain continuously reconstructs trajectory-
level semantic memory. Evaluations on the Sema-Sim benchmark
show that ReflectiChain effectively suppresses instruction rein-
terpretation, improving the Rationale Consistency Score by over
30% compared with state-of-the-art baselines. Ultimately, this
work demonstrates that reliable instruction following requires a
shift from static prompting to continuous, physically grounded,
reflective semantic reconstruction.
Index Terms—Large Language Models, LLM Agents, Embod-
ied NLP, Planning and Reasoning, Semantic Alignment

sections.text: Jia Luo Abstract —In long-horizon dynamic environments, LLM agents suffer from “Semantic-Execution Drift,” systematically reinter- preting and violating initial language constraints under physical pressure in pursuit of local success. Existing text-based reasoning paradigms lack physical grounding and temporal alignment, leading to constraint collapse. To address this problem, we pro- pose ReflectiChain, a framework that reformulates constrained planning as a trajectory-level reasoning problem by integrating an implicit latent world model with a retrospective reflection mechanism. By anticipating physical dynamics through latent rollouts and re-anchoring drifting states to the original semantic boundaries, ReflectiChain continuously reconstructs trajectory- level semantic memory. Evaluations on the Sema-Sim benchmark show that ReflectiChain effectively suppresses instruction rein- terpretation, improving the Rationale Consistency Score by over 30% compared with state-of-the-art baselines. Ultimately, this work demonstrates that reliable instruction following requires a shift from static prompting to continuous, physically grounded, reflective semantic reconstruction. Index Terms —Large Language Models, LLM Agents, Embod- ied NLP, Planning and Reasoning, Semantic Alignment I. I NTRODUCTION U SING natural language as a core constraint in em- bodied AI exposes the “Semantic Persistence Problem” in LLMs: the struggle to maintain strict fidelity to initial instructions across extended, long-horizon physical execution trajectories. This challenge is especially salient as language models are increasingly used as embodied planners and au- tonomous agents that must translate high-level instructions into situated actions [1], [2], a capability now deployed in precision-agriculture robotics and dexterous manipulation [3], [4]. We formalize “Semantic-Execution Drift,” a fundamental language grounding collapse in long-horizon agents where representational misalignment between discrete semantics and continuous physical spaces generates accumulating semantic entropy, ultimately decoupling execution from initial language constraints. Viewed as a discrete-time signal, the sequence of verbalized rationales exhibits a non-stationary degradation—a slowly time-varying bias drifting the semantic trajectory away from its intended stationary component—so that correcting SED is naturally posed as a signal-restoration problem: the reflection module acts as a recursive state estimator whose adaptive-filter correction re-anchors the drifting semantic sig- nal toward its intended stationary component. This failure mode is closely related to known limitations in long-context use, hallucination, and overconfident reasoning in large lan- guage models [5], [6]. Evaluated on the Sema-Sim benchmark, Jia Luo is with Huazhong University of Science and Technology. Fig. 1. Comparison of reasoning influence. Unlike ReAct (step-wise fo- cus) and ReflAct (internal state reflection), ReflectiChain (Ours) achieves superior long-horizon semantic alignment. By integrating world-grounded latent dynamics with retrospective rationale reflection ( A sem ), it directly mitigates semantic–execution drift and dynamically calibrates the policy, ensuring robust, degradation-free execution. ReflectiChain demonstrates that mitigating semantic-execution drift and maintaining long-horizon language grounding in LLMs requires continuous, reflective semantic reconstruction. We instantiate this mechanism within ReflectiChain and evaluate it on Sema-Sim, a complex instance of the Semantic Persistence Problem that injects dynamic natural-language policy shocks. Extensive baselines show that agents lack- ing trajectory-level semantic reprojection inevitably suffer language-grounding collapse, whereas ReflectiChain sustains trajectory-level semantic consistency under high-noise pertur- bations. This gap motivates world models over structured latent representations that efficiently simulate long- horizon dynamics under policy-driven perturbations. b) Reflection and Agentic Self-Evolution: . Reflection provides post-hoc correction via failure signals, but existing approaches are predominantly single-loop, correcting through prompt-level context without altering the underlying policy distribution [15], [16], [17], even with embodied memory and open-world planning [18], [19]. Test-time training and preference-optimization methods parameterize updates yet re- main decoupled from structured decisions and trajectory-level feedback [20], [21], [22]. Current mechanisms thus correct outputs but not the generative policy, exacerbating temporal credit assignment. We address this by introducing double-loop reflection, which turns retrospective trajectory outcomes into test-time policy updates via explicit credit assignment, evolv- ing the decision distribution rather than post-hoc reranking.

sections.heading: III. T
sections.text: RAJECTORY - LEVEL S EMANTIC R EALIGNMENT F RAMEWORK To address semantic–execution drift in long-horizon ex- ecution, we formalize planning under language constraints as a trajectory-level reasoning problem. The ReflectiChain framework eliminates the need for complex post hoc rule- based verification by integrating implicit world dynamics with language-based reasoning, thereby ensuring alignment of instructions over extended horizons. A. World-Grounded Latent Dynamics Purely language-based planning often lacks awareness of underlying physical laws. To address this, we model environ- mental evolution within a latent state space, providing physical grounding for large language models. We project heteroge- neous environmental states into continuous features z t and perform inference through a lightweight dynamic transition function: z t +1 = z t + ∆ t · f ω ( z t , a t ) . This multi-step latent rollout provides a physical feasibility likelihood p W M for the current candidate trajectory, which serves as the underlying physical context for subsequent language-based reasoning generated by the LLM. Concretely, f ω is an analytic, hand-specified transition over a six-dimensional latent state (inventory, congestion, demand, carbon, stockout, tension). It is not a pre-trained or learned- online network nor an LLM-generated simulator: coefficients ω are initialized once from environment statistics and held fixed, so no gradient training is required, and only the latent state z t —not the parameters—is advanced online by one matrix–vector product of cost O ( d 2 ) with d = 6 . This over- head is negligible relative to LLM decoding, which dominates latency; a learned variant is future work. B. Language-Constrained Inference and Reinterpretation In trajectory planning, the agent must jointly optimize linguistic priors and the physical feasibility of underlying states. We simplify this process as a joint inference objective: a ∗ t = arg max a t � log p LLM ( a t | C rule ) + λ log p W M (ˆ r | z t , a t ) � (1) where λ governs the trade-off between language-prior fidelity and physical feasibility. This joint inference explains drift: under severe physical perturbations (extremely low log p W M ), a reward-seeking agent ( λ → 0 ) is drawn toward language-level compromise to preserve the overall objective, progressively reinterpreting instructions to rationalize physically favorable yet policy-inconsistent actions—the directly observable signa- ture of semantic–execution drift at the natural-language level. C. Reflection-Based Rationale Alignment To mitigate the aforementioned linguistic degradation dur- ing trajectory evolution, we introduce a retrospective reflection mechanism. Here, rationale consistency is strictly defined as whether the agent’s verbalized reasoning throughout the interaction remains semantically aligned with the original lan- guage constraints over time. Formally, treating the rationale- embedding trajectory { h t } as a discrete-time signal, we model SED as non-stationary degradation h t = s t + v t , where s t is the intended stationary component and v t a slowly time-varying drift term; reflection then acts as a recursive estimator—akin to adaptive filtering—that predicts v t from the world-model rollout and applies a corrective measurement update to re-anchor h t toward s t —a sequential-inference step that restores the degraded semantic signal. We treat this as a core observable signal for dynamically calibrating the policy distribution: ∇ θ J ( θ ) ≈ E [ A sem ( s, a ) ∇ θ log π θ ( a | s )] (2) In this formulation, the advantage function A sem ( s, a ) is directly driven by the rationale consistency score evaluated by the reflection module. This mechanism encourages the agent to preserve semantically consistent reasoning throughout long- horizon interactions, thereby substantially reducing rationale drift under extended environmental perturbations. The Sema-Sim Benchmark To evaluate the semantic persistence of LLMs under long- horizon policies, we propose Sema-Sim (Semantic-Interactive Multi-Agent Supply Chain Simulation). Unlike traditional environments, Sema-Sim deliberately induces severe conflicts between absolute semantic constraints and local task success, forcing agents into continuous semantic compromises. The environment simulates a 4-tier supply chain (Supplier, Manufacturer, Distributor, Retailer) comprising 10 heteroge- neous nodes and approximately 30 transportation edges. These edges (certified vs. uncertified) exhibit varying latency and disruption probabilities, creating implicit risk-efficiency trade- offs. At initialization, agents are injected with 10 categories of natural language hard constraints (e.g., temporal logic, data sovereignty). As detailed in Table I, we evaluate the violation difficulty of these constraints across 3,000 heuristic trajectories to robustly quantify semantic-execution drift.

sections.heading: Baselines & Prompting
sections.text: To disentangle base-model capability from reasoning strat- egy, we select two open-source backbones (Qwen2.5-7B- Instruct, InternLM2.5-7B-Chat) and compare four progres- sively advanced strategies: • NoThinking (Direct-CoT): generates reasoning and ac- tions without cross-step memory. • ReAct [15]: a standard “think–act–observe” framework using only current observations. • ReflAct [23]: a reflective baseline that performs internal, language-level State–Goal reflection at each step. • ReflectiChain (Ours): adds forward physical grounding via a world model and dual-loop retrospective reflection, aligning with the initial semantic manifold. (We also include the classical PPO baseline without language modeling.)

sections.heading: Evaluation Metrics
sections.text: Given a trajectory τ = { ( s t , a t , r t ) } T t =1 of states, actions, and rationales, together with initial hard constraints C , we define four metrics: a) (1) Rationale Consistency Score (RCS): quantifies the semantic alignment between the agent’s step-wise reasoning and the initial constraints. Using a pre-trained DeBERTa- NLI model M NLI , we calculate the sequence-level average entailment probability: RCS = 1 T T � t =1 P entail � M NLI ( r t , C ) � (3) where the constraints C serve as the premise and the ratio- nale r t as the hypothesis. RCS is deliberately paired with the execution-based CCR below as complementary probes: RCS scores the verbalized alignment observed by reflection, whereas CCR applies symbolic, trajectory-level constraint checking, so the two mutually validate. Because NLI models may under-capture multi-step dependencies, RCS serves as a scalable semantic proxy rather than a standalone verifier; direct human-judgment correlation is left to future work. b) (2) Constraint Compliance Rate (CCR): measures trajectory-level adherence. It is defined as the ratio of steps strictly satisfying all constraints: CCR = 1 T T � t =1 � c i ∈C I ( s t , a t | = c i ) (4) where I ( · ) indicates whether the state–action pair ( s t , a t ) satisfies c i . c) (3) Trajectory Instability (TI): captures reasoning os- cillation and semantic drift during the agent’s execution. We formulate this as the average cosine distance between the representations of consecutive rationales: TI = 1 T − 1 T − 1 � t =1 (1 − cos( h t , h t +1 )) (5) where h t is the dense embedding of r t ; higher TI indicates context switching or contradiction. d) (4) Task Success (TS): evaluates the ultimate outcome via a strict binary indicator: TS = I ( s T ∈S goal ) (6) with S goal the predefined goal space. C. Performance Comparison and Temporal Dynamics Analy- sis Table II presents the overall performance of different meth- ods under long-horizon evaluation: • Limitations of Local Reflection: ReflAct improves over ReAct but its RCS stays below 70% under long-horizon pressure—local reflection alone cannot prevent semantic compromise without physical anticipation and explicit realignment. • Semantic Persistence of ReflectiChain: ReflectiChain at- tains the highest consistency with the lowest volatility (TI = 3.90); on Qwen2.5-7B it reaches RCS 88.45%, +33.0% over ReflAct. Mitigating drift thus requires both reflection and structured cross-grounding between physical trajec- tories and initial language conditions. •

sections.heading: Governance–efficiency trade-off.
sections.text: ReflectiChain’s lower TS is a deliberate operating-point choice, not an incapac- ity: λ is a tunable penalty coefficient weighting constraint fidelity against reward, tracing a Pareto frontier from reward-seeking ( λ → 0 ) to constraint-dominant ( λ ≫ 1 ) ex- ecution. The reported point uses large λ to isolate drift mitigation, and reducing λ recovers ReAct-like reward seeking. Adaptive constraint weighting relaxes constraints the world model certifies as physically infeasible, so the agent deviates only when strict satisfaction is provably impossible, restoring task completion under genuine in- feasibility. Microscopic Analysis: Instruction Reinterpretation and Self-Alignment To investigate why even ReflAct exhibits RCS degrada- tion, we analyze 200 high-pressure trajectories. Models rarely exhibit abrupt “rule forgetting”; instead they systematically reinterpret instructions via (1) goal drift, (2) exception injec- tion, and (3) temporal relaxation. sections.heading: State Restatement vs. Trajectory Reflection:
sections.text: To rule out prompt engineering, a variant enforcing rule restatement (ReAct + Rule Verbalization) raises RCS only marginally to 58.2%, far below ReflectiChain—simple linguistic restatement cannot resist semantic divergence under physical pressure. Removing the world model (w/o WM) reduces the agent to a text-based reflective system akin to ReflAct, dropping CCR to 75.10%; removing retrospective reflection (w/o Retro) collapses RCS to 58.12%. C ONCLUSION In this work, we formalize the failure mode of semantic- execution drift in long-horizon agents and propose Reflec- tiChain , a closed-loop framework bridging discrete semantic constraints and continuous interaction dynamics via retrospec- tive reflection. Empirical evaluations on the Sema-Sim bench- mark demonstrate that ReflectiChain effectively mitigates “in- struction reinterpretation” under non-stationary perturbations, establishing that reliable instruction following requires contin- uous reflective realignment rather than static prompting.
